input_signals.hypothesis: Growth that outpaces the balance sheet is growth the existing asset base delivered; when a cheap firm has expanded revenue faster than assets over five years, its mid-cycle earning power is scaling without absorbing new capital, whereas a cheap firm whose assets grew faster than sales is buying revenue and will not deliver that earning power to owners.
input_signals.reasoning: The sign pathology is eliminated at the source: both legs of the difference are growth rates of strictly positive quantities, so no firm can be ranked as disciplined because its cumulative profit was negative. It is also not the asset-growth anomaly in disguise — a firm growing assets rapidly can rank highly provided revenue grew faster — which is precisely the difference between the investment factor and the capital-efficiency mechanism this tests.

input_signals.name: LiquidityBuffer_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness only pays if the firm survives long enough for mid-cycle earning power to reassert itself; a liquid balance sheet is the insurance that lets a cheap firm ride out the trough without a dilutive rescue, so the value premium should be concentrated among cheap firms holding a real cash buffer.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the collinear DuPont conjunction — which could not have discriminated between competing explanations of the champion — with a survivability channel that is orthogonal to profitability measures entirely, and it is structurally different from the failed net-cash-to-price signal: cash enters as a bounded balance-sheet conditioner rather than as the valuation numerator, so the signal cannot be hijacked by tiny cash-burning firms whose net cash dominates their market value. Together with the accepted operating-business-price proposal it separates two distinct roles for cash: correcting the price of operations versus insuring the operating business.

input_signals.hypothesis: The two balance-sheet conditions are jointly necessary rather than substitutable: a cash-rich firm whose operations still devour capital, and a capital-light firm with no liquidity to survive the trough, both fail to deliver mid-cycle earning power to owners, so the weaker of the two readings should govern.
input_signals.reasoning: Together with Signals 1 and 2 this completes a clean three-way test of how the two proven conditioners should be combined — additively, as one netted quantity, or conjunctively — and MIN is the only one of the three that cannot be reproduced by any linear function of the inputs. It is the appropriate structure if the mechanism is a survival-and-retention requirement rather than a graded characteristic.

input_signals.hypothesis: If the cash conditioner works because the market underprices balance-sheet cash, then removing cash from the price should absorb the effect; if it works because liquidity is insurance that lets a cheap firm survive to realize its earning power, then removing cash from the price should sharpen it by measuring the operating business more accurately.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the decisive attribution test between the two strongest cash-related results in the archive — cash as a conditioner (3.6% alpha) and cash netted from the denominator (2.5%) — and the two readings imply opposite outcomes, so the result is informative either way rather than a grid cell. It matters for the final recommendation because a mispricing-of-cash interpretation and an insurance interpretation imply different exposures and different robustness out of sample.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What protects a cheap firm is not gross cash but its liquidity relative to the claims against it: the share of cash in cash-plus-debt measures whether the firm's financial position lets it wait out a downturn, and cheapness should pay in proportion to that slack.
input_signals.reasoning: Gross cash intensity earned 3.6% alpha and low leverage earned only 1.6%, so the open question is whether the liquidity effect survives being expressed net of the obligations that offset it — a firm holding large cash against larger debt has no real buffer. The ratio is bounded in the unit interval by construction and therefore avoids the sign and scale pathologies that sank the earlier net-cash-to-price formulation, while preserving full coverage.

input_signals.name: CapitalReplacementRunway_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, dp), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The balance-sheet condition that protects normalized cheapness is how many years of capital replacement a firm could fund from cash already in hand; a cheap firm with several years of runway will reach the recovery in its mid-cycle earning power without raising outside money, while one whose cash covers only months of capital consumption must dilute or borrow first.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the dimensionally incoherent stock-minus-flow difference with a ratio of two dollar quantities whose quotient has a genuine unit — years of replacement capital funded — and it is not a relabeling of cash intensity, because it equals cash-to-assets divided by depreciation-to-assets and therefore moves with both winning conditioners rather than either alone. It states the combination of the archive's two best conditioners as one interpretable economic quantity instead of a statistical blend, which is the substantive version of the idea the critic rejected.

input_signals.name: LiquidAssets_Plus_NormalizedEarningsYield_Composite
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(che, at), RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))
input_signals.hypothesis: If liquid balance-sheet composition genuinely strengthens cheapness rather than merely adding to it, then the multiplicative conditioning form should beat an equally weighted composite of the same two ingredients; the composite is the honest benchmark, and it is a defensible signal in its own right because it buys firms that are cheap on mid-cycle earning power, liquid, or both.
input_signals.reasoning: This uses exactly the two inputs of the archive's best signal (cash intensity and the normalized earnings yield, alpha 3.6%) in a strictly equal-weighted additive form, so it resolves the identification question the entire run rests on — whether the conditioning is a true interaction or a repackaged two-signal composite — without the weighting distortion of nested rank sums. Its portfolio will also be far less concentrated than the product's, so if it matches the product's alpha with a higher Sharpe the additive form is the better final recommendation, and if it falls materially short the interaction claim is confirmed.
